newsitem.title: UK: Oil recovers from U.S. gasoline futures sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Oil recovers from U.S. gasoline futures sell-off.

text.p: Oil prices on Thursday slipped and then recovered from a sell-off in the gasoline market in the United States.
London September Brent crude futures finished just three cents down at $18.94 a barrel, close to an eight-week price high.
In New York West Texas Intermediate front-month futures finished at $20.12 a barrel, down 18 cents, but well above the day's low of $19.65.
Oil prices, sensitive during the summer months to demand for gasoline in the U.S., have found support from rising demand and hiccups in refinery operations.

Speculators, active buyers of the New York gasoline contract in the past week, scrambled to close positions before the August contract expired on Thursday. It ended more than three cents a gallon down on the day

But fundamental strength in gasoline transferred to September, the next month, which finished slightly up, allaying fears the expiry would signal an end to the strength of the unleaded motor fuel contract.
Output disruptions and strong demand have tightened prompt supply of gasoline.
Data released by the American Petroleum Institute recorded a feverish 8.7 million barrels per day (bpd) implied gasoline demand over the past month.
Tosco Corp shut down a gasoline producing unit at its 250,000 bpd Bayway refinery on Wednesday after detecting a leak, a source close to the refinery said.
The New Jersey facility normally produces 130,000 bpd of gasoline and houses the largest catalytic cracking unit in the world.

A fire on Thursday at the Curacao refinery in Venezuala, which supplies heavy volumes of oil products to the U.S. market, cut output by 130,000 bpd, though officials hoped to limit the losses by the weekend.
A lack of clear news from the United Nations also disturbed markets, brokers said.

The U.N. was expected to approve Iraq's aid-distribution plan, the final hurdle to a resumption of Iraqi exports under the U.N. food-for-oil deal, by the weekend, well-placed sources at the organisation said.
"We have said that we would approve it by the end of July and I would say give or take a day or so we will have it done," said a senior U.N. official involved in the review of the deal.
But the lack of a firm start date has left crude markets still fearfull they will run short of supplies.
Iraq has made approval of the aid plan a condition of restarting oil exports under the "oil-for-food" deal.
Once it is approved, Iraq must submit for approval by the U.N.'s overseers a price formula and oil sales contracts, a process that is expected to take no more than a few days.

The scheme allows Iraq to sell slightly more than $2 billion of oil over 180 days in two equal installments. The clock started ticking on June 8, which means Iraq must sell $1 billion of oil by September 5 or forego some of its allotment.
Though Iraq officials had said it was looking for the U.N. to start the clock ticking from the date of approval of the aid plan, Baghdad appeared to drop that issue on Wednesday.
